title: Combinatorial optimization of connected UAV communication bridges for emergency response
abstract: We present a combinatorial optimization problem for the strategic deployment of UAVs equipped with 5G antennas to assist rescue operations in regions hit by natural disasters. Our goal is to optimize the placement of UAVs to provide coverage in flying ad-hoc networks among given candidate sites. Our formulation aims to maximize signal coverage and minimize interference while ensuring network connectivity. To mitigate interference effects, we incorporate the use of multiple frequencies. We formulate this problem as an integer quadratic program (IQP). We present numerical solutions obtained via the CPLEX solver and conduct a preliminary analysis of the problem's scalability in realistic network configurations. Our findings reveal a significant exponential increase in Time-to-Solution (TTS) as the number of sites grows, which poses a critical challenge in urgent, time-sensitive scenarios. To address this issue, approximate suboptimal solutions can be produced by enforcing a time limit on the solver. Although these solutions are not optimal, they preserve connectivity in most cases, providing a practical trade-off between solution quality and computational times that remain within feasible limits for real-time UAV redeployment. Recognizing the limitations of classical solvers in these contexts, we explore quantum computing as a promising alternative. Specifically, we reformulate the problem as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem, suitable for most quantum algorithms. Through high-performance computing emulation, we show that the quantum adiabatic algorithm (QAA) can accurately solve small-scale instances, paving the way for future application of quantum computing to large-scale, time-critical optimization problems in disaster response.
summary: This work tackles the critical optimization challenge of deploying UAVs for emergency communication networks by formulating it as a complex combinatorial problem. Due to the exponential scaling of classical solvers, the authors reformulate the problem into a QUBO suitable for quantum computation. The research demonstrates the potential of quantum algorithms to solve these time-sensitive, large-scale optimization problems in real-time disaster response scenarios.
main_problem: The paper addresses the combinatorial optimization problem of strategically deploying UAVs to establish connected communication bridges in disaster zones.
main_result: Classical solvers exhibit exponential time-to-solution scaling, necessitating the reformulation of the problem as a QUBO suitable for quantum algorithms like the Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm (QAA).
method: The problem is formulated as an Integer Quadratic Program (IQP) and subsequently mapped to a QUBO, which is then analyzed using both classical solvers (CPLEX) and quantum emulation (QAA).
model_or_system: The system involves UAVs in a flying ad-hoc network (FANET) needing to maximize signal coverage and maintain connectivity via a backbone structure while mitigating interference using multi-frequency assignments.
key_observables: Signal coverage, network connectivity (backbone/leaves), interference levels, and Time-to-Solution (TTS).
important_parameters: Number of candidate sites ($N$), number of available drones ($V$), number of backbone nodes ($B$), and number of frequencies ($F$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that quantum computing offers a scalable alternative to classical solvers for this time-critical optimization task; approximations are made regarding higher-order interference overlaps.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the network components (coverage, connectivity, interference) and show performance metrics for QAA on small instances, demonstrating the feasibility of quantum approaches.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the c-BUP problem, formulates it as an IQP/QUBO, analyzes the classical computational bottlenecks (exponential TTS), and then proposes and tests the quantum adiabatic algorithm approach.
why_interesting: The direct mapping of a complex, real-world combinatorial optimization problem (UAV placement) onto a QUBO framework and testing it with quantum algorithms makes it highly relevant for quantum algorithm development in applied physics.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Description of the connected ad-hoc network of UAVs modeled in this work. In panel (a), we show the basic building block of the network, a UAV equipped with a 5G antenna that provides coverage to the ground. The blue blob describes the full shape of the signal approximated as a sphere, while the green area shows the effective coverage provided by the UAV. Panel (b) shows the connectivity of the network. UAVs within the same blob can receive and transmit air-to-air signal to each other. Red wiggly pulses describe the backbone network, while orange ones indicate links that end there. Gray pulses indicate that it is not possible to establish a connection link between the two UAVs....

Fig. 2. Illustration of the two graphs involved in the c-BUP problem. The air-to-air graph GB is shown at the top, while the interference graph GV is shown at the bottom of the picture. A solution of this problem with V = N is shown as an example in Fig. 1 panel (d).

Fig. 5. Solution of the problem for the instance (16, 12, 3, 2). On the left, we represent the connectivity, while to the right we show the frequency assignment. In this case with F = 2, we notice two interference conflicts.

Fig. 6. Solution of the problem for the instance (16, 12, 3, 3). On the left, we represent the connectivity, while to the right we show the frequency assignment. In this case with F = 3, we notice that all the interference is avoided.

Fig. 4. Number of leaves disconnected from the backbone in the presence or absence of the cubic term for several configurations. This plot shows the importance of that term for the overall connectivity. All the configurations have been chosen in such a way that a fully connected solution is feasible, meaning that the number of connections is smaller than Cmax.
